Snake Pass: The Pennine's Dark Horse

The A57 Snake Pass connecting Sheffield and Manchester is one of England's great Pennine crossings. Less famous than the Cat and Fiddle but equally rewarding, Snake Pass offers a genuinely atmospheric ride through some of the Peak District's wildest moorland. The name comes from the road's serpentine route rather than any wildlife, though it does twist through the landscape with satisfying regularity.

The Route

Snake Pass runs for approximately 20 miles between Ladybower Reservoir and Glossop. From the Sheffield side, it starts at the dramatic Ladybower and Derwent Reservoirs (the famous Dambusters practice site), climbs through the Woodlands Valley, and crosses the summit at the Snake Pass Inn (512 metres) before descending to Glossop.

The Character

Snake Pass feels wilder and more remote than the Cat and Fiddle. The road passes through dark forests, skirts peat-black reservoirs, and crosses bleak moorland. In low cloud or drizzle, the atmosphere is extraordinary — you feel like you're riding through a Brontë novel. The road surface is generally good, though standing water is common after rain.

Riding Tips

  • Direction: East to west (Sheffield to Glossop) gives the best views and most dramatic approach
  • Best conditions: Clear autumn mornings when the moors turn golden
  • Hazards: Standing water, blind crests, and sheep. The road is exposed and weather can change quickly
  • Winter: Frequently closed due to snow and ice — check conditions before setting out
Snake Pass in autumn mist is one of England's most atmospheric motorcycle experiences. The moors glow golden, the reservoirs reflect the sky, and the road disappears into the cloud ahead.

Combining with Other Routes

Snake Pass works perfectly as part of a Peak District loop. From Glossop, head south on the A624 to Chapel-en-le-Frith, then east on the A623 through the dramatic Winnats Pass to Castleton. Continue through the Hope Valley back to Ladybower. This 45-mile circuit covers the best of the Dark Peak and can include a stop at the Ladybower Inn for lunch.

History

The road was built as a turnpike in 1821, replacing packhorse routes across the moors. The Snake Pass Inn at the summit has served travellers for two centuries. The Woodlands Valley section was flooded in the 1940s to create Ladybower Reservoir — several villages disappeared beneath the water, and in dry summers their ruins sometimes emerge from the receding water line, adding another layer of atmosphere. faq.q: How long is Snake Pass and where does it run?
faq.a: Snake Pass runs for approximately 20 miles between Ladybower Reservoir and Glossop, connecting Sheffield and Manchester. From the Sheffield side it starts at the dramatic Ladybower and Derwent Reservoirs, climbs through the Woodlands Valley and crosses the summit at the Snake Pass Inn at 512 metres.

faq.q: What is the best direction to ride it?
faq.a: Ride east to west, from Sheffield to Glossop, for the best views and the most dramatic approach. Clear autumn mornings when the moors turn golden are the ideal conditions. In low cloud or drizzle the atmosphere is extraordinary, like riding through a Bronte novel across bleak Pennine moorland.

faq.q: Is Snake Pass open in winter?
faq.a: Not reliably. Snake Pass is frequently closed in winter due to snow and ice, so always check conditions before setting out. The road is exposed and the weather can change quickly, while standing water is common after rain and blind crests and sheep add to the hazards year-round.

faq.q: Can I combine Snake Pass with other roads?
faq.a: Yes. It works perfectly as part of a Dark Peak loop. From Glossop head south on the A624 to Chapel-en-le-Frith, then east on the A623 through the dramatic Winnats Pass to Castleton, and back through the Hope Valley to Ladybower. This 45-mile circuit can include a lunch stop at the Ladybower Inn.
